name: Passive-Active Voice Ratio
description: Analyzes the balance and switching frequency between active and passive voice constructions. AI models, heavily aligned for neutrality and objectivity, tend to drastically overuse the passive voice to avoid assigning direct agency or blame (e.g., 'mistakes were made' rather than 'we made mistakes'), or they maintain an unnaturally consistent ratio throughout a text. Human writers switch voices much more dynamically based on emotional intent, emphasis, and narrative pacing.
algorithm: Syntactic Agency Mapping and Voice Transition Variance
mechanism: This algorithm uses dependency parsing to classify every clause in the text as either Active (Subject-Verb-Object) or Passive (Object-Verb-by-Subject). It calculates two primary metrics: the absolute ratio of Passive to Active sentences, and the 'Voice Transition Rate' (how often the text switches between the two). Large Language Models (LLMs) are RLHF-trained to sound authoritative, safe, and objective. This training inadvertently penalizes the use of first-person active voice in many contexts, causing the AI to rely heavily on passive constructions ('It is important to note that...', 'The data was analyzed...'). Even when prompted to write actively, AI texts often settle into a stagnant, mathematically consistent ratio of voice usage. Human writers are highly erratic: they might write a purely active, aggressive introductory paragraph, switch to a heavily passive methodology section, and return to an active conclusion. Human voice-switching is driven by narrative rhythm and rhetorical focus, creating clustered bursts of active or passive sentences. The system calculates an 'Agency Artificiality Score' by measuring both the over-reliance on passive structures and the lack of organic clustering in voice transitions.
useCase: Crucial for analyzing corporate communications, academic essays, and news articles, distinguishing the sterile, artificially objective tone of a machine from the dynamic, intentional voice shifts of a human author.
strengths:
• Highly effective at detecting AI writing that attempts to sound 'professional' or 'academic', as these prompts almost always trigger the AI's passive voice bias.
• Difficult for average users to bypass, as most prompt engineers focus on vocabulary rather than deeply grammatical agency structures.
limitations:
• Prone to false positives in scientific papers, lab reports, or technical manuals where human authors are strictly required by style guides (e.g., APA formatting guidelines of the past) to use the passive voice exclusively.
• Less effective on casual, highly conversational texts (like text messages) where passive voice is rarely used by either AI or humans.
parameters:
Analysis: Dependency Parsing for Subject-Verb-Object Agency
Metric: Passive/Active Ratio and Voice Transition Clustering
Output: 0-100 Agency Artificiality (Voice Rigidity) Score
accuracy: Moderate to High — 75-85% accuracy. A highly reliable metric for formal, educational, and professional writing contexts where AI over-indexes on 'objective' safety.

references.title: Uchendu, A. et al. (2020). Authorship Attribution for Neural Text Generation. EMNLP.
Guo, B. et al. (2023). How Close is ChatGPT to Human Experts? Comparison Corpus, Evaluation, and Detection. NeurIPS.
